title: The Man of Charms and Talismans: one line in a dictionary, two books under another man's name
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Great Mosque of Kufa, the balance of natures
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the dating of the Jabirian corpus is itself contested, Kraus placing much of it later than the attributed lifetime
stops.campa: In the mosque city on the Euphrates the workshops of Arabic alchemy take their first shape, and a body of writing gathers under the name of Jabir ibn Hayyan: sulphur and mercury, the balance of natures, the making of things by art. Two centuries later a Cordoban compiler will set this material into his chapters on the properties of stones and metals without ever crossing the sea to see the place. What travels is the book, not the man, and it travels westward only in copies.
sources: Ritter and Plessner, Picatrix critical apparatus (1933/1962), source-tradition analysis
David Pingree, 'Some of the Sources of the Ghayat al-hakim', JWCI 43 (1980)
suggested_refs: The Jabirian corpus as a source stratum of the Ghayat al-Hakim; not a stop on any journey of Maslama's own

stops.name: Harran, the temples of the seven
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Sabian survival at Harran is attested in Arabic sources, the transmission route into the Ghaya is inferred
stops.campa: North of the Syrian plain the people the Muslim jurists call Sabians keep their planetary temples standing into the tenth century, seven houses for seven wanderers, each with its metal, its incense, its hour, its prayer. Their invocations pass into Arabic through intermediaries whose names are half lost. The doctrine that a star's power can be drawn down into a prepared image and fixed there is the working assumption of the whole talismanic science, and Harran is where the Arabic tradition says it was kept alive.
sources: Ritter and Plessner on Sabian material in the Ghayat al-Hakim
Fahd; van Bladel on the Harranian Sabians
suggested_refs: Sabian planetary invocations preserved in the Ghayat al-Hakim's fourth book

stops.name: Old Basra, the Brethren of Purity
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; both the Basra base and the tenth-century dating of the Rasa'il are debated, and the old garrison site lies some 15 km southwest of the modern city
stops.campa: On the ground of the old garrison town southwest of the later city, a company of authors who sign themselves the Brethren of Purity assemble their epistles: number, music, the soul, the spheres, and the making of talismans. They hold that every earthly thing answers to something above it, and that the chain of answering can be worked in both directions. The Cordoban book will take that correspondence as its first principle and quarry the epistles directly. Who the Brethren were, and when exactly they wrote, the sources do not agree.
sources: Godefroid de Callatay on the Ikhwan al-Safa and the Picatrix
Ritter and Plessner, source apparatus
Wikipedia, 'Basra' (location of the original garrison settlement)
suggested_refs: The Rasa'il Ikhwan al-Safa as a principal quarry of the Ghayat al-Hakim

stops.name: Baghdad, the Nabataean Agriculture
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Ibn Wahshiyya's milieu is attested, the composition address is not
stops.campa: In the caliphal capital Ibn Wahshiyya produces the Kitab al-Filaha al-Nabatiyya, presenting it as a translation out of an ancient Nabataean tongue: farming, and with it the magical botany of plants sown under one star and cut under another. The claim of deep antiquity is part of the method, not an accident of it. The Andalusian compendium will lift from the book freely and keep the borrowed antiquity, because a talisman inherited from the ancients is worth more than one invented last week.
sources: Toufic Fahd, edition and study of the Nabataean Agriculture
Ritter and Plessner on its use in the Ghayat al-Hakim
suggested_refs: Kitab al-Filaha al-Nabatiyya, quarried by the Ghaya for its magical botany

stops.name: Madinat al-Zahra, the sciences inside the patronage
stops.date_confidence: attested for the palace city, begun 936-940 under Abd al-Rahman III; no document places Maslama within it
stops.campa: Abd al-Rahman III raises a palace city on the slope west of Cordoba, and into it come physicians, astronomers, translators, and men who cast horoscopes for the caliph's household. The occult sciences are not marginal here. They sit inside the patronage, next to the medicine and the astronomy, drawing salaries and copying fees. The compendium that will gather the whole talismanic art into one book is written in this decade by someone moving through this culture. No document places him inside these walls.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Medina Azahara' (foundation and coordinates)
Maribel Fierro, 'Abd al-Rahman III', on the caliphal court and its sciences
suggested_refs: The excavated terraces of Madinat al-Zahra, sacked in the fitna of 1010

stops.name: Cordoba, the Rutbat al-Hakim written
stops.date_confidence: contested; standard Fierro and Pingree dating gives 339-342 AH (950-953), while English Wikipedia's al-Majriti page dates the work to circa 1009, a figure irreconcilable with everything else on the same page
stops.campa: He writes first the Rutbat al-Hakim, the Sage's Step, on alchemy: the transmutation of metals, the elixir, the operations set down in order. The larger book will announce itself as begun when this one was finished, which makes the two a single project of about a decade. The dates given for it do not agree with each other. One line of the tradition puts it in the early 950s; another reference work puts it around 1009, half a century after its author is dead on any reckoning.
stops.quote: the two works are the 'Sage's Step/The Rank of the Wise' (Rutbat al-hakim, ?1009) and the Picatrix
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Picatrix' (the 343 AH hinge year)
English Wikipedia, 'Maslama al-Majriti' (the circa 1009 dating)
Fierro 1996, title, which names both works
suggested_refs: Rutbat al-Hakim, the alchemical companion volume to the Ghayat al-Hakim

stops.name: Cordoba, the Ghayat al-Hakim completed
stops.date_confidence: attested by the text's own introduction (348 AH); scholars dispute whether the colophon records true completion or a later scribal insertion, and a competing consensus dates the work to the mid-eleventh century
stops.campa: The Ghayat al-Hakim is finished: four books, some four hundred pages, the twenty-eight mansions of the moon, the images to be cut under each planet, the suffumigations, the prayers addressed to the seven, and the theory that holds the apparatus together. Whoever writes it has read the Brethren of Purity, the Nabataean Agriculture, the Hermetic books, and the Sabian rites, and has put them into one working handbook. The text states its own year of completion. It states no name.
stops.quote: the author of the Arabic original states in its introduction that he completed the book on 348 AH
stops.quote_source: Wikipedia, 'Picatrix', on the chronological problem with the al-Majriti attribution
sources: Internal dating of the Arabic Ghayat al-Hakim, reported in English Wikipedia, 'Picatrix', citing David Pingree, JWCI 43 (1980), p. 2
Hellmut Ritter, ed., Ghayat al-Hakim, Studien der Bibliothek Warburg 12 (1933)
suggested_refs: The introduction of the Arabic Ghayat al-Hakim, carrying the 348 AH date

stops.name: The Great Mosque of Cordoba, a man of charms and talismans
stops.date_confidence: inferred; his residence in Cordoba is attested by the nisba and by Ibn al-Faradi, his presence at the mosque is not, and the year is set at the accession of al-Hakam II because the campa names his reign
stops.campa: Under al-Hakam II the Friday mosque anchors a city of jurists, traditionists, and a caliph who buys books by agent from Damascus to Basra. Somewhere in that crowd moves Maslama ibn Qasim, whom a younger Cordoban will one day enter in a dictionary of scholars with a single descriptor: sahib al-ruqa wa-l-tilasmat, a man of charms and talismans. No teacher of his is named, and no student either. Nothing records where he lived in the city or where he worked. The trade is recorded; the man is not.
stops.quote: One recent study in Studia Islamica suggests that the authorship of this work should be attributed to Maslama b. Qasim al-Qurtubi, who died 964 CE (353 AH) and, according to Ibn al-Faradi, was 'a man of charms and talismans'.
stops.quote_source: Wikipedia, 'Picatrix', authorship section, relaying Ibn al-Faradi via Fierro (1996)
sources: Ibn al-Faradi, Ta'rikh ulama al-Andalus, as analyzed by Maribel Fierro, Studia Islamica 84 (1996), pp. 87-112 (article not reached; relayed via English Wikipedia, 'Picatrix')
suggested_refs: The prayer hall of al-Hakam II's extension to the Great Mosque, built 961-976

stops.name: Cordoba, the death in 353
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year (353 AH) via Fierro; month, day, and place within the city are unrecorded anywhere
stops.campa: He dies in the year 353. The notice that records it gives the year and the trade and nothing else: no age, no illness, no burial ground, no successor. Cordoba is at its height, the caliphate intact, al-Hakam II on the throne with a library of hundreds of thousands of volumes, and one of its citizens leaves the city with a line and a half of ink behind him. No tomb is recorded then or later, and no shrine grows. The books now thought to be his carry no name at all in their earliest copies.
sources: Ibn al-Faradi, Ta'rikh ulama al-Andalus, as reported by Fierro, Studia Islamica 84 (1996)
suggested_refs: Ibn al-Faradi's entry on Maslama ibn Qasim, the only biographical notice known

stops.name: Cordoba, the name in full
stops.date_confidence: retrospective marker, not an event; the general medina is used as the pin because no address is recorded
stops.campa: The dictionary gives him in full: Maslama ibn al-Qasim ibn Ibrahim ibn Abd Allah ibn Hatim al-Qurtubi al-Zayyat. Four generations of fathers, a city, a trade in oil. The nisba says Cordoba, and Cordoba is where he lived, but it separates him from nobody. The astronomer he will be confused with is entered in the sources as al-Majriti al-Qurtubi, born at Madrid and settled here. Both men are the Cordoban. What tells them apart is the father's name and the year of death, and nothing else.
stops.quote: Maslama Ibn al-Qasim Ibn Ibrahim Ibn Abd Allah Ibn Hatim al-Qurtubi al-Zayyat
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Picatrix'
English Wikipedia, 'Maslama al-Majriti' (the astronomer's own full name, which includes al-Qurtubi)
suggested_refs: The onomastic tangle: al-Majriti al-Qurtubi al-Faradi versus Ibn al-Faradi the biographer

stops.name: Kairouan, the young Cordoban heads east
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the journey and the stop; the year within the early 990s is not fixed
stops.campa: In the early 990s a young Cordoban named Ibn al-Faradi takes the road east, as ambitious Andalusians do, to collect hadith from the mouths of the men who hold it. He stops at Kairouan, first of the great Maghribi schools on the way, and reads with whoever will teach him. He is gathering the credentials that will make his own book authoritative, and his book will contain the only sentence anyone will ever find about the man of charms and talismans who died at Cordoba a generation before his own birth.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Ibn al-Faradi' ('In the early 990s, he travelled to the East and pursued his studies in Kairouan, Cairo, Mecca and Medina')
suggested_refs: The Mosque of Uqba at Kairouan, first school of the eastern journey

stops.name: Cairo, the discipline of the chain
stops.date_confidence: attested as a stop on his eastern journey; the year is inferred from the early-990s frame
stops.campa: He goes on to Cairo, some twenty years after the Fatimids founded it, a city building its own claim to be the center of Islam. He reads with the scholars he can reach and writes down their chains of transmission. The method he is learning is the method of the biographical dictionary: who taught whom, who was reliable, who died in what year. It is an accounting discipline applied to knowledge, and it will preserve one obscure Cordoban talisman-maker for as long as the paper lasts.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Ibn al-Faradi'
suggested_refs: The biographical-dictionary method as an instrument of preservation

stops.name: Mecca, study at the Haram
stops.date_confidence: attested that he studied at Mecca and Medina; whether he performed the pilgrimage is not stated in any source consulted
stops.campa: He continues to the Hijaz and studies at Mecca and Medina, the last stage of an eastern journey that gives an Andalusian scholar the authority of the far schools. Whether he performs the pilgrimage while he is there is not stated in the sources that survive, though a man at Mecca in the 990s who did not would be a curiosity. He turns west again with his notebooks. The dictionary of the scholars of al-Andalus, when he writes it, will rest on this journey and on the archives of his own city.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Ibn al-Faradi' (studies at Mecca and Medina; the hajj is not asserted)
suggested_refs: The eastern rihla as a credentialing journey for Andalusi scholars

stops.name: Cordoba, the dictionary of the scholars
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the Ta'rikh was compiled after his return and before his death in 1013, with no closer date available
stops.campa: Home in Cordoba, he compiles the Ta'rikh ulama al-Andalus, the history of the scholars of al-Andalus: hundreds of entries, each with name, teachers, specialty, and year of death, arranged so a reader can check whether a chain of transmission holds. Under the letter mim he enters Maslama ibn Qasim, dead in 353, and calls him a man of charms and talismans. He is not praising him. A biographer of the pious noting an irregular trade does not know he is writing the only line by which the man will ever be found.
sources: Ibn al-Faradi, Ta'rikh ulama al-Andalus, as reported by Fierro (1996) via English Wikipedia, 'Picatrix'; the Arabic text was not consulted
suggested_refs: Ta'rikh ulama al-Andalus, the sole surviving witness to Maslama ibn Qasim

stops.name: Cordoba, the biographer killed in the sack
stops.date_confidence: attested as to date; the place of his death within the sacked city is not recorded
stops.campa: Berber troops break into Cordoba and sack it, and Ibn al-Faradi is killed in the streets of his own city on the twentieth of April. The caliphate does not recover. The palace city west of the walls is already looted and burning, and the library of al-Hakam II is being sold and scattered. His dictionary survives him in copies, by a margin nobody measured at the time. Without those copies the man of charms and talismans has no name and no date, and no other document in al-Andalus supplies either.
sources: Standard biographical notices of Ibn al-Faradi's death during the fitna of al-Andalus
Wikipedia, 'Ibn al-Faradi'
suggested_refs: The Berber sack of Cordoba, 1013, and the dispersal of the caliphal library

stops.name: Majrit, the astronomer born on the frontier
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the birthplace is inferred from the nisba, the year given as circa 950 across reference works
stops.campa: In the frontier town of Majrit, a garrison on the road up from Toledo, Abu al-Qasim Maslama ibn Ahmad is born around the year 950. He will take his nisba from this place and carry a second one, al-Qurtubi, from the capital where he spends his working life. In the year the Ghayat al-Hakim announces its own completion he is a boy of about nine. That arithmetic is the first objection to the attribution his name will bear for six hundred years, and nobody performs it until the twentieth century.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Maslama al-Majriti'
Said al-Andalusi, Tabaqat al-Umam, as relayed there
suggested_refs: The Alcazaba of Majrit, under the later Palacio Real, Madrid

stops.name: Cordoba, the school of the astronomer
stops.date_confidence: attested as to activity under al-Hakam II and after; the pin marks the caliphal administrative quarter generally, the Alcazar de los Reyes Cristianos on the site being a fourteenth-century Christian foundation
stops.campa: Grown, Maslama al-Majriti becomes the leading astronomer of al-Andalus. He corrects and adapts the tables of al-Khwarizmi to the meridian of Cordoba, works on Ptolemy's Planisphaerium, and gathers a school around him in the caliphal quarter. Ibn al-Saffar and Ibn al-Samh come out of it, and through them the astrolabe and the tables pass into the taifa courts. Later lists of his students add men born fifty and sixty years after his death, and the lists are copied forward without anyone doing the subtraction.
stops.quote: According to Said al-Andalusi, he was the best mathematician and astronomer of his time in al-Andalus.
stops.quote_source: Wikipedia, 'Maslama al-Majriti', citing Said al-Andalusi, Tabaqat al-Umam
sources: English and Spanish Wikipedia, 'Maslama al-Majriti' / 'Maslama al-Mayriti'
Wikipedia, 'Abu al-Salt' and 'Al-Turtushi' (both born 50-60 years after al-Majriti's death, and therefore removed from the student list)
suggested_refs: The Cordoban recension of al-Khwarizmi's zij; the Arabic Planisphaerium

stops.name: Cordoba, the astronomer dies and his biographers say nothing
stops.date_confidence: conventional; 398 AH / 1007, with 1004-1008 given across modern reference works
stops.campa: The astronomer dies at Cordoba, the year usually given as 398 of the Hijra, with the civil war that will end the caliphate a few years off. His biographers are thorough men and they are thorough about him: the tables, the Planisphaerium, the school, the students, the corrections, the surveying. Not one of them, in his own century or the next, says he wrote a book on talismans. This is not an argument from nothing. These are writers who list everything a scholar produced, and for this book they list nothing.
sources: English and Spanish Wikipedia, 'Maslama al-Majriti'
English Wikipedia, 'Picatrix', on the silence of the near-contemporary biographies (summarizing Pingree and Fierro)
suggested_refs: The argument from biographical silence, central to the modern reattribution

stops.name: Denia, the astronomy carried east
stops.date_confidence: attested that Ibn al-Saffar worked and died at Denia, d. 1035; the year of his arrival is inferred from the collapse of Cordoba
stops.campa: Cordoba falls into the fitna and the school scatters. Ibn al-Saffar carries his master's astronomy east to Denia on the Mediterranean coast, under the taifa there, and dies in the town in 1035. Astrolabe treatises, tables, the practical geometry of instruments: this is the legacy the sources actually record moving out of al-Majriti's hands, and it moves through this port. The book that will one day be hung on his name is not in the baggage, and no student of his ever mentions it.
sources: Biographical notices of Ibn al-Saffar's career and death at Denia
suggested_refs: Ibn al-Saffar's treatise on the use of the astrolabe, transmitted from Denia

stops.name: Madrid, a daughter invented for him
stops.date_confidence: attested that the legend cannot be traced earlier than the 1920s; the precise year of its first appearance is not established
stops.campa: Nine centuries after the astronomer's death a daughter is invented for him: Fatima de Madrid, astronomer, working beside her father on the tables. No medieval source knows her. The story cannot be traced earlier than the 1920s, and scholarship now treats it as a modern accretion rather than a lost tradition recovered. It fastens onto the same name that had already collected a book its owner did not write. Madrid gets an astronomer daughter, and al-Majriti gets a second thing he did not do.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Maslama al-Majriti', on the Fatima de Madrid legend and its dating
suggested_refs: The twentieth-century Fatima de Madrid legend, a second accretion on the same name

stops.name: Cairo, al-Jildaki writes the name onto the book
stops.date_confidence: contested; his death is given as 743 AH / 1342-43 in the standard reckoning and as 762 AH / 1361 by Brockelmann, whom the Picatrix literature follows
stops.campa: In Mamluk Cairo the alchemist Aydamur al-Jildaki, who has travelled seventeen years through Iraq, Anatolia, Yemen, the Maghrib, and Syria collecting books, sets down the earliest known attribution of the Rutbat al-Hakim to Maslama al-Majriti. Close to four centuries stand between him and the composition. He needs an author for an anonymous work and finds a Cordoban with a reputation for mercury and a school behind him. The name goes on, and it does not come off for six hundred years.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Picatrix', summarizing the manuscript tradition via Holmyard
Wikipedia, 'Al-Jildaki' (the 743/1342-43 dating and the Brockelmann alternative)
suggested_refs: Al-Jildaki's alchemical commentaries, the earliest witness to the Majriti attribution

stops.name: Qal'at Ibn Salama, the Muqaddima written
stops.date_confidence: attested; he sheltered at the fortress 1375-1379 and drafted the Muqaddima during that stay, the coordinates approximate a hilltop some three miles south of Frenda
stops.campa: Sheltering in a fortress on a hilltop south of Frenda, out of politics for four years, Ibn Khaldun writes the Muqaddima. In the chapters on the occult sciences he treats the Ghayat al-Hakim and names its author as Maslama al-Majriti of Cordoba, the mathematician. He does not verify it, and there is nothing available with which to verify it. What he does is lend it his own name, and every later writer who repeats the attribution repeats it on his word. After him the question is closed for five hundred years.
sources: Ibn Khaldun, Muqaddima, chapter on the occult sciences
Wikipedia, 'Qalat Ibn Salama' (the 1375-1379 retreat and the fortress's position south of Frenda)
suggested_refs: The Muqaddima's chapter on talismans and the sciences of letters

stops.name: Al-Azhar, Cairo, the attribution hardens into record
stops.date_confidence: attested for his Cairo decades, 1382 to his death in 1406; al-Azhar stands for his teaching milieu generally, since he held posts at several madrasas
stops.campa: Ibn Khaldun goes east and spends his last decades at Cairo, teaching, judging, and revising the great book again and again until his death in 1406. Every copy made in the schools of this city carries the attribution forward with the rest of the text. A statement repeated in the Muqaddima is no longer a statement; it is a fact of the record, and copyists do not annotate facts of the record with the doubt that produced them. The Arabic book itself, meanwhile, circulates thinly and quietly.
sources: Standard biography of Ibn Khaldun's Cairo years
English Wikipedia, 'Picatrix', on the fixing of the attribution
suggested_refs: Manuscript copies of the Muqaddima produced in the Cairo madrasas

stops.name: Toledo, the Castilian commission
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the 1256-1258 window by the Latin prologue's own testimony; no source specifies where in the itinerant court the work was done, and the pin stands for the translation culture
stops.campa: Alfonso X of Castile, who keeps a court full of translators and an appetite for the sciences of the vanquished, orders the Ghayat al-Hakim put into Castilian. The Latin prologue of the version that follows dates the work between 1256 and 1258. Who did the translating is recorded nowhere, in either the Latin or the Spanish tradition. The Castilian survives only in fragments; the Latin made from it survives whole, and under a corrupted title, Picatrix, the book enters Europe with the wrong author's name on it.
stops.quote: According to the prologue of the Latin translation, Picatrix was translated into Spanish from the Arabic by order of Alphonso X of Castile at some time between 1256 and 1258.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Picatrix', citing David Pingree, Picatrix: The Latin Version (1986), p. 3
Bakhouche et al., Picatrix: Un traite de magie medievale (Brepols), pp. 32-33
suggested_refs: The Latin prologue of the Picatrix, sole witness to the date of the Castilian version

stops.name: Seville, the court that does not sit still
stops.date_confidence: attested for the court's itinerancy in these years; the commissioning location is not specified in any source
stops.campa: The court that commissions the translation does not sit still. It moves between Toledo, Seville, and Murcia with the king, its scriptorium travelling in boxes, producing law codes, chronicles, star tables, lapidaries, and books of games in the same years and often by the same hands. The talismanic compendium is one commission among many. Alfonso is not collecting curiosities. He is having the library of al-Andalus rendered into a language his own chancery can read, a generation after the cities it came from were taken.
stops.quote: En torno a 1256, Alfonso X ordeno traducir al castellano y al latin el tratado arabe de magia talismanica.
sources: Spanish Wikipedia, 'Picatrix'
Standard accounts of Alfonso X's court itinerary and translation patronage
suggested_refs: The Alfonsine scriptorium and its output of law, history, astronomy, and magic

stops.name: Krakow, the manuscript that carries the Latin text
stops.date_confidence: the manuscript is medieval and undated here; the library building at this address was constructed 1931-1939, so the pin marks the present repository, not the copying place
stops.campa: A Latin manuscript of the Picatrix, nearly complete, comes to rest in the university library at Krakow. It is the backbone of every modern edition of the Latin text, and without it the Latin tradition would be a matter of fragments collated against fragments. The copy is medieval; the building that now holds it went up in the 1930s; the shelf mark is younger than the paper by six centuries. The name attached to the text, where a name appears at all, is still Maslama's.
sources: David Pingree, Picatrix: The Latin Version of the Ghayat al-Hakim, Studies of the Warburg Institute 39 (London, 1986)
Wikipedia, 'Jagiellonian Library' (address and building date)
suggested_refs: The Jagiellonian manuscript, base text of Pingree's Latin edition

stops.name: Vatican Library, the witnesses among the condemned arts
stops.date_confidence: general repository marker; the manuscripts are medieval to Renaissance and individually undated here
stops.campa: Further Latin witnesses lie in the Vatican collections, along with the astrological manuscripts that drew on them. Nothing here is unique, and Pingree's apparatus will use these copies for collation rather than as a base text. The holdings show circulation: the book moved between courts and cardinals' libraries as a working text on images and hours, copied by people who meant to use it, and it was kept by the institution that condemned the practice, catalogued and shelved among the sciences.
sources: Pingree's apparatus in Picatrix: The Latin Version (1986), listing Vatican witnesses
suggested_refs: Vatican Reg. lat. 1283a and the Alfonsine magical corpus

stops.name: Florence, the book read by the Platonists
stops.date_confidence: attested for the publication of De vita libri tres in 1489; the Picatrix as its source is standard in Walker and Yates but is not carried by every reference work
stops.campa: Marsilio Ficino publishes De vita libri tres at Florence in 1489, and its third book, on drawing down the life of the heavens, works the same ground as the Ghayat al-Hakim: images, planetary hours, the capture of celestial influence in prepared matter. Giovanni Pico della Mirandola numbers the book among the magical authorities of his own project. Neither man knows the author's name, because at this date nobody does. They know Maslama, and Maslama, whichever one they mean, is the wrong answer.
sources: D. P. Walker, Spiritual and Demonic Magic from Ficino to Campanella
Wikipedia, 'Marsilio Ficino' (De vita libri tres, 1489)
suggested_refs: De vita coelitus comparanda, book III of Ficino's De vita libri tres

stops.name: Munich, a working text for practitioners
stops.date_confidence: general repository marker; the Bavarian copy is medieval to Renaissance and not closely dated here
stops.campa: Another Latin copy sits among the Bavarian holdings, evidence that German-speaking readers of astrology had the book in hand well before any critical edition existed. The Picatrix circulates as practical literature: what image to cut, in what metal, under which hour, with what suffumigation and what words spoken over it. Its readers are not historians of philosophy. They are men who mean to make something, and the Cordoban whose name they do not have wrote it for exactly that purpose.
sources: Pingree's apparatus in Picatrix: The Latin Version (1986)
suggested_refs: German astrological and magical miscellanies incorporating Picatrix material

stops.name: London, four astrologers and one manuscript
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the chain of ownership is recorded, the year is a marker for the Elizabethan and Stuart span it covers
stops.campa: A single Latin manuscript passes down a chain of English practitioners: Simon Forman the astrologer-physician, then Richard Napier, then Elias Ashmole, then William Lilly, each of them reading it as a live working text and each believing it the work of an Arab called Maslama. Six hundred years after the compendium was finished at Cordoba, its instructions are still being followed in a language its author never heard, under a name he never bore. None of the four asks who Maslama was.
sources: The manuscript chain as recorded in the atlas file maslama_al_majriti.journey.json
Standard accounts of the Forman-Napier-Ashmole-Lilly papers
suggested_refs: The Ashmole manuscripts at the Bodleian, carrying the English Picatrix chain

stops.name: El Escorial, the Zidan library comes up the mountain
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to relevance; the seizure at sea in 1612 and the incorporation at the Escorial in 1614 are attested, but no Ghayat al-Hakim manuscript is confirmed among them
stops.campa: A Spanish fleet takes the library of the Saadian sultan Zidan at sea in 1612, and in 1614 the manuscripts are carried up to the monastery library in the sierra above Madrid, the largest sudden arrival of Arabic books in Christian Spain. Whether any copy of the Ghayat al-Hakim is among them has never been established. What is established is the shape of the transmission: Andalusi and Maghribi learning returning to the peninsula as spoil, catalogued by men who mostly could not read it.
sources: History of the Zidan library capture (1612) and its incorporation at the Escorial (1614)
suggested_refs: The Arabic manuscripts of the Real Biblioteca del Monasterio de El Escorial

segments.name: The Arabic Recovered, the Name Undone

stops.name: Istanbul, the Arabic text found again
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the identification is credited to Wilhelm Printz in the 1920s in Ritter's own account, without a fixed year
stops.campa: In the Ottoman library holdings of Istanbul, Wilhelm Printz identifies an Arabic manuscript of the Ghayat al-Hakim. For six and a half centuries Europe has known only the Latin and the lost Castilian behind it. Now there is a text to compare them against. The source analysis and the internal dating both wait on this manuscript; without it nobody knows that the book states its own year of completion. Ritter will print his Arabic edition from it eight years later.
stops.quote: a 400-page Arabic book of magic and astrology, which most scholars assume was originally written in the middle of the 11th century
stops.quote_source: Wikipedia, 'Picatrix', introductory section, reporting a dating consensus that contradicts the text's own 348 AH statement
sources: Ritter's account of Printz's identification, in the introduction to the 1933 Arabic edition
English Wikipedia, 'Picatrix'
suggested_refs: The Istanbul manuscript of the Ghayat al-Hakim, base of Ritter's edition

stops.name: Hamburg, the Warburg volume twelve
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1933 edition; the imprint is Leipzig and Berlin, and Ritter himself was resident at Istanbul from 1926 to 1949 and was not in Germany when the volume appeared
stops.campa: Hellmut Ritter's edition of the Arabic Ghayat al-Hakim appears as volume twelve of the Studien der Bibliothek Warburg, the series of a private library in Hamburg built around the survival of images. Ritter has lived at Istanbul since 1926 and is not in Germany to see it printed; the volume comes out at Leipzig and Berlin. Within months of publication the library that gave the series its name is packed into two ships and sent to London, ahead of the regime.
sources: Hellmut Ritter, ed., Ghayat al-Hakim, Studien der Bibliothek Warburg 12 (Leipzig and Berlin, 1933)
Wikipedia, 'Hellmut Ritter' (Istanbul residence 1926-1949)
Wikipedia, 'Warburg Institute' (the 1933 relocation)
suggested_refs: The Warburg-Haus at Heilwigstrasse 116, Hamburg, emptied in 1933

stops.name: Woburn Square, London, Pseudo-Magriti on the title page
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1962 publication; the institute reached Woburn Square only in 1958, having passed through Thames House in 1934 and the Imperial Institute Buildings in 1937
stops.campa: The library, reassembled in London and moved twice more before it reaches Woburn Square in 1958, becomes the institutional home of the book. In 1962 Ritter and Martin Plessner publish the German translation under the title Picatrix: Das Ziel des Weisen von Pseudo-Magriti. The qualifier is doing the whole of the work. Thirty-four years before anyone proposes another name, the editors state on the title page that the author of record is not the author.
sources: Hellmut Ritter and Martin Plessner, 'Picatrix': Das Ziel des Weisen von Pseudo-Magriti (London: Warburg Institute, 1962)
Wikipedia, 'Warburg Institute' (the sequence of London addresses)
suggested_refs: The 1962 German translation, the first full modern rendering of the Arabic

stops.name: Brown University, the Latin edition
stops.date_confidence: attested; the series is Studies of the Warburg Institute 39, not the Surveys and Texts series sometimes cited
stops.campa: David Pingree, at Brown, spends years on the Latin text and produces the critical edition, Studies of the Warburg Institute volume thirty-nine, in 1986. He has already traced the sources: Hermetic, Sabian, Ismaili, Indian, Nabataean, the Brethren of Purity. He has already published on the lost Castilian stage between the Arabic and the Latin. The one thing his apparatus does not settle is the name on the cover, which he prints, with the field's reservations, as Maslama al-Majriti, because nothing yet exists to put in its place.
sources: David Pingree, Picatrix: The Latin Version of the Ghayat al-Hakim, Studies of the Warburg Institute 39 (London, 1986)
Pingree, 'Some of the Sources of the Ghayat al-hakim', JWCI 43 (1980)
Pingree, 'Between the Ghaya and Picatrix. I: The Spanish Version', JWCI 44 (1981)
suggested_refs: Pingree's collation apparatus, the standard tool for all later attribution work

stops.name: Madrid, Fierro names the other Maslama
stops.date_confidence: attested for the article; the CSIC pin is Fierro's later institutional home and stands for the scholarly context, not the place of composition
stops.campa: Maribel Fierro publishes in Studia Islamica an article on the Batini and Sufi currents of tenth-century al-Andalus and, in the course of it, proposes a different Maslama. Ibn al-Faradi's line about a man of charms and talismans, dead in 353, fits the milieu that produced these two books. The astronomer, a child of nine in the year the larger book claims completion and silent in his own biographies, does not. The title of the article states the conclusion without hedging it.
stops.quote: If this suggestion is correct it would place the work in the context of Andalusian sufism and batinism.
sources: Maribel Fierro, 'Batinism in Al-Andalus. Maslama b. Qasim al-Qurtubi (died 353/964), Author of the Rutbat al-Hakim and the Ghayat al-Hakim (Picatrix)', Studia Islamica 84 (1996), pp. 87-112; the article itself was behind a paywall and is relayed through the footnotes of English Wikipedia, 'Picatrix'
suggested_refs: Studia Islamica 84 (1996), pp. 87-112, the pivot publication of the reattribution

stops.name: University Park, Pennsylvania, the old name on the new translation
stops.date_confidence: attested; the volume is catalogued under Maslamah ibn Ahmad al-Majriti despite citing Fierro within its own apparatus
stops.campa: Dan Attrell and David Porreca publish the first complete English translation of the Latin Picatrix, made from Pingree's edition. Twenty-three years after the reattribution, and citing it in their own apparatus, they catalogue the volume under Maslamah ibn Ahmad al-Majriti. The old name is a finding aid now: readers search for it, libraries file under it, and the correction sits inside the covers of the book that carries it. Nothing in the volume disputes Fierro. The name is simply what the record says.
sources: Maslamah ibn Ahmad al-Majriti [as catalogued], Picatrix: A Medieval Treatise on Astral Magic, trans. Dan Attrell and David Porreca (Pennsylvania State University Press, 2019), ISBN 9780271082127
English Wikipedia, 'Picatrix', fnn. 1 and 15
suggested_refs: The 2019 Penn State translation, catalogued under the superseded attribution

stops.name: Cordoba, what is left of him
stops.date_confidence: retrospective marker, not an event
stops.campa: What survives of him is one line in a dictionary of scholars, a year of death, a trade, and two books that carry his name in no copy anyone has found. He has no tomb, no birth date, no teacher, no student, no street. The book now thought to be his was translated for a Castilian king, made into Latin for Renaissance Europe, worked over by English astrologers, edited in German, and englished in Pennsylvania, and through the whole of it, it was signed by another man.
sources: Ibn al-Faradi, Ta'rikh ulama al-Andalus, via Fierro (1996)
English Wikipedia, 'Picatrix'
suggested_refs: The absence of any tomb, shrine, or monument for either Maslama
